The constitution of Community Recovery, as its working draft of September 2026 words it: every clause stands at an address of its own in the draft's own words, and the lines above the clauses are signposts, never the constitution. A recovery-oriented working draft guided by the 33 LERO Standards, co-produced and not yet adopted; it takes effect only when Community Recovery's members adopt it at a General Meeting. How it is read and answered is the family's law, function:constitution.

1._: Why Community Recovery exists and what it stands on — what this document is, the organisation's name, purpose and vision, and the framework, values and principles every later section answers to.
About this Constitution — its working status, what it sets out, and the core commitment.
1.1:
Working status
This is a co-produced working draft. It should be reviewed by Community Recovery members, the interim Leadership Group and an appropriately qualified governance adviser before formal adoption or use for incorporation, funding or banking purposes.
1.2:
About this Constitution
This Constitution sets out why Community Recovery exists, how people can belong and contribute, how volunteer leadership is developed, and how the organisation will make decisions and remain accountable. It is intended to bring the LERO Standards to life through proportionate governance, lived experience leadership and recovery-oriented practice.
1.3:
Core commitment
Community Recovery exists to support community members to learn, grow and live their new life in recovery. Recovery and wellbeing come before organisational roles or commitments.

2._: 1. Name, Purpose and Vision — the organisation's name, its purpose and vision, who it primarily serves, and what makes it distinctive.
2.1:
1.1 Name
The name of the organisation is Community Recovery, referred to in this Constitution as “Community Recovery” or “the organisation”.
2.2:
1.2 Purpose
Community Recovery exists to support community members to learn, grow and live their new life in recovery.
Through lived experience leadership, peer support, volunteering, personal development and community participation, Community Recovery creates opportunities for people to develop Connectedness, Hope, Identity, Meaning and Empowerment.
Community Recovery supports people to build stability, discover their strengths, pursue their aspirations and create lives that are meaningful to them.
2.3:
1.3 Vision
Community Recovery envisions communities where people affected by broad experiences of addiction and substance use, homelessness, involvement with the criminal justice system and mental health challenges can build stability, develop meaningful lives, contribute to their communities and thrive in ways they choose.
Community Recovery seeks to foster connectedness, hope, a positive and self-defined identity, meaning and empowerment, together with opportunities for personal, vocational and professional development.
2.4:
1.4 Who Community Recovery primarily serves
Community Recovery primarily exists for people in recovery from addiction and substance use, and for people rebuilding their lives following homelessness, prison or other involvement with the criminal justice system, and mental health challenges.
Family members, supporters, allies and community partners who share the organisation’s values may also belong and contribute, provided that lived experience remains central to leadership and decision-making.
2.5:
1.5 What makes Community Recovery distinctive
Community Recovery is led by lived experience and seeks to make recovery visible through learning, contribution, volunteering, meaningful occupation and personal and professional development.
Community Recovery places each person’s recovery and wellbeing before any voluntary or work commitment. It uses peer mentoring, peer coaching and peer-supported approaches to foster compassionate cultures of care, growth and transformational change.

3._: 2. Recovery Framework, Values and Principles — CHIME and its five components, recovery before role, how each person is seen and met, and how the organisation stands among others.

1._: CHIME, the recovery framework the organisation is founded on, and its five components — clauses 2.1 to 2.6.
1.1:
2.1 CHIME as the foundational recovery framework
Community Recovery is founded upon Connectedness, Hope, Identity, Meaning and Empowerment, known as CHIME.
CHIME guides the organisation’s purpose, culture, relationships, volunteering, leadership, governance, activities and decisions. Community Recovery believes recovery is strengthened when people experience belonging, develop hope for the future, build positive identities, find meaning and purpose, and gain greater choice and control over their lives.
1.2:
2.2 Connectedness
We foster relationships, peer support, belonging, community participation and social inclusion.
1.3:
2.3 Hope
We create realistic opportunities for positive change, growth and a fulfilling future.
1.4:
2.4 Identity
We respect each person’s culture, values, strengths and right to define themselves beyond past experiences or labels.
1.5:
2.5 Meaning
We support people to find purpose through interests, goals, learning, contribution, volunteering, work and community life.
1.6:
2.6 Empowerment
We promote choice, autonomy, confidence, capability, shared decision-making and self-determination.

2._: Recovery before role, and lived experience as leadership — clauses 2.7 and 2.8.
2.1:
2.7 Recovery First
No member, volunteer or leader is expected to place organisational responsibilities above their recovery, health, wellbeing or essential personal responsibilities.
2.2:
2.8 Lived Experience Leadership
We recognise lived experience as a valuable source of expertise, credibility, insight, leadership and hope.

3._: How each person is seen and met — clauses 2.9 to 2.12.
3.1:
2.9 Strengths and Assets
We begin with people’s gifts, skills, relationships, resources, interests and aspirations, not deficits or labels.
3.2:
2.10 Growth and Development
We support personal, social, educational, vocational and professional development in ways that are meaningful to each person.
3.3:
2.11 Inclusion
We welcome difference, challenge stigma and discrimination, and seek to remove barriers to belonging, participation and leadership.
3.4:
2.12 Compassion
We treat people with dignity, kindness and understanding, while supporting honest reflection and appropriate accountability.

4._: How the organisation stands among others — clauses 2.13 to 2.15.
4.1:
2.13 Community
We believe sustainable recovery is strengthened through relationships, mutual support, active citizenship and strong communities.
4.2:
2.14 Independence
We collaborate with others while protecting Community Recovery’s identity, lived experience voice and freedom to act according to its purpose and values.
4.3:
2.15 Co-production
We develop Community Recovery with members, not for them, and seek to involve people affected by decisions in shaping those decisions.

2._: Who we are to each other — members, volunteers and the people who lead on members' behalf.

1._: 3. Membership, Participation and Volunteering — who may be a member, members' rights and responsibilities, how participation may change, and volunteering as a pathway with its levels and process.
1.1:
3.1 Membership
Community Recovery is a membership-led organisation. Membership is open to any person aged 18 or over who supports its purpose and values and wishes to contribute positively to the community.
Membership creates belonging and participation. It does not require a person to undertake a formal volunteer role.
1.2:
3.2 Rights of members
To be treated with dignity, respect and fairness.
To participate in activities, subject to available capacity and appropriate safety arrangements.
To contribute ideas, feedback and lived experience knowledge.
To attend and vote at General Meetings, with one vote per eligible member.
To nominate themselves for suitable volunteer and leadership opportunities.
To seek learning, growth and development opportunities.
To prioritise recovery and wellbeing and to step back without stigma.
1.3:
3.3 Responsibilities of members
Support the purpose and values of Community Recovery.
Treat others with dignity, kindness and respect.
Contribute to a safe, inclusive and hopeful community.
Respect privacy and confidentiality.
Raise safeguarding or safety concerns through appropriate routes.
Avoid behaviour that exploits, coerces, discriminates against or harms others.
1.4:
3.4 Participation may change
Community Recovery recognises that participation may fluctuate because of recovery, health, family, work or personal circumstances. Members who take a break remain valued and should be welcomed back without stigma or disadvantage wherever possible.
1.5:
3.5 Volunteering as a pathway
Community Recovery recognises volunteering as a pathway for contribution, personal growth, learning, leadership development and active citizenship. Leadership is exercised through volunteering and service to the community, not status or authority.
1.6:
3.6 Volunteer levels
Community Recovery may provide different forms of volunteering according to responsibility and risk:
Entry-level or activity volunteers may undertake agreed practical or community roles. A DBS check will only be required where the role and relevant rules make it appropriate.
Peer Leader volunteers are formal volunteers who support peer growth, belonging, participation and development through peer support, mentoring, coaching, activities or groups.
Lived Experience Leader volunteers are formal volunteers who nurture organisational growth, steward values and support governance, representation and sustainable development.
Leadership Group members are formal volunteers who govern Community Recovery on behalf of members.
1.7:
3.7 Formal volunteer process
Formal volunteer roles, including Peer Leaders, Lived Experience Leaders and Leadership Group members, will follow an agreed volunteer process. Requirements will be proportionate to the role and may include:
Application or expression of interest.
Role description and volunteer agreement.
Induction and required training.
DBS checks where required for the role.
Safeguarding and confidentiality commitments.
Ongoing support, supervision and reflective practice.
Commitment to relevant policies, procedures and working practices.

2._: 4. Leadership and Governance — the Leadership Group, who sits on it and who may, how lived experience stays in the lead, how long people serve, and how they leave.

1._: The Leadership Group and who sits on it — clauses 4.1 to 4.3.
1.1:
4.1 Leadership Group
Community Recovery shall be governed by an elected Leadership Group acting on behalf of members. During the start-up period, the interim Leadership Group may be appointed by mutual agreement as described in clause 4.8.
The Leadership Group shall steward the organisation’s purpose, CHIME framework, values, assets, governance, safety, accountability and sustainable development.
1.2:
4.2 Composition
The Leadership Group shall have a minimum of 5 and a maximum of 12 members, comprising:
A Lived Experience Co-Chair.
A Community Co-Chair.
A Treasurer, where appointed.
A Secretary, where appointed.
Between 2 and 9 additional Leadership Group members, subject to the overall maximum of 12.
1.3:
4.3 Co-Chairs
The Co-Chairs share responsibility for inclusive leadership, sound governance and constructive meetings. Neither Co-Chair has authority to govern alone.
The Lived Experience Co-Chair will ordinarily be a Lived Experience Leader volunteer and will champion lived experience leadership, recovery values and members’ voices.
The Community Co-Chair will ordinarily be a Peer Leader volunteer and will champion community participation, volunteer engagement, peer growth and inclusion.

2._: Who may serve, and how lived experience stays in the lead — clauses 4.4 to 4.6.
2.1:
4.4 Eligibility
A person joining the Leadership Group must be an active member, complete the formal volunteer process, be willing to undertake governance responsibilities, uphold Community Recovery’s values and meet role-related safeguarding, training and DBS requirements.
2.2:
4.5 Protecting lived experience leadership
Community Recovery shall remain led by lived experience. At least 75% of Leadership Group members should have relevant lived or living experience connected to the organisation’s purpose.
The Leadership Group should predominantly comprise active Community Recovery volunteers, with Peer Leader and Lived Experience Leader volunteers appropriately represented wherever possible. Volunteers gain greater influence through representation and responsibility, not through additional votes at General Meetings.
2.3:
4.6 Officer functions
As Community Recovery develops, members should work towards electing Leadership Group members. Unless members decide otherwise, the Leadership Group may allocate Treasurer, Secretary and other officer responsibilities from among those elected or appointed, taking account of skills, development goals, capacity and recovery-first practice.

3._: How long people serve, the start-up arrangement, and leaving — clauses 4.7 to 4.9.
3.1:
4.7 Flexible service
Leadership is developmental and dynamic. People may nominate themselves to serve for up to one year. During the start-up phase, appointments should normally be reviewed after six months to consider continuation, a change of role, additional support, stepping down or movement towards member-led elections.
No person should be pressured to over-commit. A volunteer may reduce responsibilities or step back when needed, with proportionate arrangements made to maintain safety and continuity.
3.2:
4.8 Transitional arrangements
During the initial development phase, Leadership Group members and officer functions may be appointed by mutual agreement of the existing initiating group. This is a time-limited, practical arrangement while membership, volunteer systems and democratic processes develop.
The interim Leadership Group shall review the arrangement at least every six months and work towards transparent nominations and member-led elections as soon as Community Recovery has sufficient membership, participation and governance capacity.
3.3:
4.9 Leaving or removal from the Leadership Group
A Leadership Group member may resign at any time. Membership may also end following a fair process where a person is unable to fulfil the role, persistently breaches the Constitution or policies, creates unmanaged conflicts of interest, or presents a serious risk to people or the organisation.
Except where immediate safeguarding action is necessary, the person should be told the concerns, offered support and an opportunity to respond, and informed of the decision and any review route.

3._: How we decide, answer to one another and keep each other safe — decisions, meetings and accountability, then safeguarding, wellbeing and psychological safety.

1._: 5. Decision-Making, Meetings and Accountability — how decisions are made, the meetings with their quorum and records, accountability and learning, and dialogue, boundaries and conflicts of interest.
How decisions are made — clauses 5.1 and 5.2.
1.1:
5.1 Decision-making principles
Community Recovery is committed to transparent, inclusive and recovery-oriented decision-making. Decisions must support the organisation’s purpose, CHIME framework, values and recovery-first commitment.
The organisation will involve members, volunteers and people affected by decisions wherever reasonably possible. It will seek consensus before moving to a vote.
1.2:
5.2 Voting
At General Meetings, each eligible member present has one vote. Volunteers do not receive additional votes because of their role.
Where consensus cannot be achieved, a simple majority will decide unless this Constitution requires a higher threshold. Abstentions are not counted as votes cast.
If a Leadership Group vote is tied, the Co-Chairs should pause the decision where possible, support further dialogue and bring back a revised proposal. If an urgent tied decision remains, it will not proceed unless an agreed risk or safeguarding procedure requires immediate action.

2._: The meetings, their quorum and their records — clauses 5.3 to 5.7.
2.1:
5.3 Annual General Meeting
Community Recovery shall hold an Annual General Meeting each year where reasonably practicable. The meeting shall:
Receive a report on activities, learning and impact.
Receive an accessible financial report.
Review progress against the purpose, CHIME framework and values.
Provide space for members to question and influence the Leadership Group.
Elect Leadership Group members when democratic elections are operational.
Consider properly submitted constitutional amendments or other significant decisions.
2.2:
5.4 Special General Meetings
A Special General Meeting may be called by the Leadership Group or following a written request from at least five members or 20% of the membership, whichever is lower. The request must explain the matter requiring a decision.
Reasonable notice and accessible information should be provided, except where urgent safety or legal considerations require a shorter process.
2.3:
5.5 Leadership Group meetings
The Leadership Group shall meet as often as needed for effective governance, volunteer support, activity delivery and organisational development.
During the early development phase, meetings are expected to be more frequent to establish pace, rhythm, policies, practice and safe delivery. As Community Recovery matures, the Leadership Group should normally meet at least every two months, or more frequently where required.
2.4:
5.6 Quorum
A Leadership Group meeting is quorate when at least half of its current members are present, including at least one Co-Chair wherever reasonably possible, and never fewer than three people.
A General Meeting is quorate when at least five eligible members or 20% of eligible members, whichever is lower, are present. The Leadership Group should keep these arrangements under review as membership grows.
2.5:
5.7 Records and communication
The organisation shall keep proportionate records of key meetings, decisions, actions, finances and declared conflicts of interest.
Key decisions and progress should be communicated to members in plain language, while protecting personal, confidential and safeguarding information.

3._: Answering to one another, and learning — clauses 5.8 and 5.9.
3.1:
5.8 Accountability
The Leadership Group is accountable to members and must act in the best interests of Community Recovery. Volunteers, Peer Leaders, Lived Experience Leaders and Leadership Group members are accountable for following agreed volunteer arrangements, policies, safeguarding requirements and role boundaries.
3.2:
5.9 Learning, reflection and continuous improvement
Community Recovery views recovery, volunteering, leadership and community development as continuing learning processes. Members, volunteers and leaders are encouraged to provide feedback, reflect on successes and challenges, and contribute to organisational improvement.

4._: Dialogue, boundaries and conflicts of interest — clauses 5.10 to 5.13.
4.1:
5.10 Open, peer-supported dialogue
Community Recovery adopts an open, peer-supported dialogue approach to learning, accountability and problem-solving. This means:
Making space for each person’s perspective and lived experience.
Listening before reaching conclusions.
Speaking honestly, respectfully and with compassion.
Avoiding blame, shame and unnecessary hierarchy.
Naming concerns early and considering their impact on people and relationships.
Seeking shared understanding, learning, repair and practical next steps.
Using formal safeguarding, complaints or disciplinary routes when dialogue alone would be unsafe or insufficient.
4.2:
5.11 Boundaries and connected communities
Community Recovery recognises that members and volunteers may also be friends, relatives, peers or part of shared recovery and community networks. These connections can strengthen trust and belonging, but may also create overlapping roles, competing loyalties, confidentiality concerns or power imbalances.
People are expected to remain aware of their responsibilities, declare relevant relationships or conflicts, seek guidance early and agree proportionate boundaries. Not every boundary concern is misconduct. Concerns should first be approached through reflection and open dialogue where safe and appropriate.
Suspected exploitation, abuse, coercion, discrimination, serious confidentiality breaches or other safeguarding concerns must be addressed through the appropriate formal process.
4.3:
5.12 Compassionate accountability
Community Recovery balances kindness with responsibility, support with accountability, and understanding with proportionate action. It seeks to help people learn and repair relationships while protecting individuals, the wider community and the organisation.
4.4:
5.13 Conflicts of interest
Leadership Group members and volunteers shall declare any actual, potential or perceived conflict of interest as soon as possible. The Leadership Group shall record the conflict and agree proportionate action, which may include seeking advice, restricting access to information, or the person not taking part in discussion or voting.

2._: 6. Safeguarding, Wellbeing and Psychological Safety — the commitment to safety, safeguarding, the wellbeing framework, psychological safety, trauma-informed practice, and recovery first in practice.
2.1:
6.1 Commitment
Community Recovery is committed to environments that are safe, welcoming, inclusive, trauma-informed and recovery-oriented. Safety, wellbeing and psychological safety are foundations for participation, learning, growth and community development.
2.2:
6.2 Safeguarding
Community Recovery will safeguard adults, children and young people in line with relevant law, policy and recognised good practice. Safeguarding is a shared responsibility, and concerns must be raised through agreed routes.
Volunteer checks, training, supervision and responsibilities will be proportionate to each role. A DBS check will be required where the role and applicable rules make this appropriate; it will not automatically be required for every form of volunteering.
2.3:
6.3 Wellbeing and recovery framework
Community Recovery recognises emotional wellbeing, social connection, physical wellbeing, personal growth, meaning and purpose as foundations for recovery and thriving.
Community Recovery may adopt and develop practical, evidence-informed wellbeing frameworks and approaches that support these aims and remain consistent with CHIME. Detailed practice frameworks will be maintained outside the Constitution so they can be learned from and improved over time.
2.4:
6.4 Psychological safety
Community Recovery seeks to create spaces where people can share experiences, express different views, ask for help, admit mistakes, raise concerns, contribute ideas and learn without fear of humiliation, discrimination, exclusion or unnecessary judgement.
Psychological safety does not mean avoiding challenge or overlooking harmful behaviour. It means concerns are raised respectfully, people are heard, and proportionate action is taken.
2.5:
6.5 Trauma-informed practice
Community Recovery will seek to understand the impact of adversity and trauma, promote emotional and physical safety, strengthen trust and collaboration, support choice and empowerment, and avoid unnecessary re-traumatisation.
2.6:
6.6 Recovery First in practice
Members and volunteers are encouraged to ask for support, reduce responsibilities or step back when needed. Such decisions should be respected and supported without stigma, while maintaining proportionate arrangements for safety and continuity.

4._: What we hold and who we work with — money, assets, partnerships and independence.

1._: 7. Finance, Assets and Resources — stewardship, non-profit use, banking and authorisation, records and reporting, and assets.
1.1:
7.1 Stewardship
Community Recovery shall manage money, property and other resources responsibly, transparently and solely in support of its purpose, values and long-term sustainability.
1.2:
7.2 Non-profit use
Income and property must not be distributed to members. This does not prevent:
Reimbursement of properly authorised expenses.
Reasonable payment for goods or services supplied under a transparent and properly authorised arrangement.
Employment or contractual arrangements approved in accordance with conflicts-of-interest procedures.
1.3:
7.3 Banking and authorisation
Community Recovery shall maintain one or more bank accounts in the organisation’s name. The Leadership Group shall set clear financial authorisation limits and controls. Wherever reasonably practicable, at least two authorised people shall approve significant expenditure or financial commitments.
1.4:
7.4 Records and reporting
Accurate financial records shall be maintained. Accessible financial information shall be provided to the Leadership Group and presented to members at the Annual General Meeting.
1.5:
7.5 Assets and intellectual property
Equipment, funds, grants, materials, digital assets, branding and intellectual property acquired or developed for Community Recovery shall be held for the benefit of the organisation and used consistently with its purpose.

2._: 8. Partnerships and Independence — collaboration, co-production in partnerships, and independence of voice.
2.1:
8.1 Collaboration
Community Recovery values collaboration with communities, voluntary organisations, public services, education providers, businesses, funders and other partners where this benefits members and supports the organisation’s purpose.
2.2:
8.2 Co-production in partnerships
Wherever reasonably possible, Community Recovery will involve members, volunteers and people with lived experience in shaping partnerships, funded work and activities that affect them.
2.3:
8.3 Independence and voice
Community Recovery shall remain an independent lived experience recovery organisation. Partnership or funding arrangements must not fundamentally conflict with the organisation’s purpose, CHIME framework, recovery-first principle, community accountability or commitment to lived experience leadership.
The Leadership Group shall consider power, influence, reputation, sustainability and mission drift before entering significant partnerships or funding arrangements.

5._: How the rules themselves are kept, changed and ended — policies, amendments, dissolution, adoption and review.

1._: 9. Policies and Working Practices — the supporting policies, and how they stand beneath the Constitution.
1.1:
9.1 Supporting policies
The Leadership Group shall adopt proportionate policies and working practices needed for safe and effective operation. These may include safeguarding, health and safety, finance, data protection, confidentiality, equality and inclusion, complaints, conflicts of interest, volunteering, boundaries, lone working, risk management and social media.
1.2:
9.2 Relationship to the Constitution
Policies and role descriptions support the Constitution but do not replace it. They may be reviewed and updated by the Leadership Group following appropriate consultation. If a policy conflicts with this Constitution, the Constitution takes precedence unless a legal requirement provides otherwise.

2._: 10. Constitutional Amendments — how amendments are made, and the principles no amendment may break.
2.1:
10.1 Making amendments
This Constitution may be amended by a resolution at a General Meeting called with reasonable notice of the proposed wording. An amendment requires at least two-thirds of votes cast by eligible members present.
2.2:
10.2 Protecting core principles
Any amendment must remain consistent with Community Recovery’s purpose, CHIME framework, recovery-first principle and commitment to lived experience leadership. Where a proposed amendment may affect legal status, regulated activity, charitable use of assets or funding conditions, appropriate advice should be sought before adoption.

3._: 11. Dissolution — the decision to dissolve, and where remaining assets go.
3.1:
11.1 Decision to dissolve
Community Recovery may be dissolved only by a resolution passed at a General Meeting called specifically for that purpose. Dissolution requires at least two-thirds of votes cast by eligible members present.
3.2:
11.2 Remaining assets
After all liabilities are met, remaining assets shall not be distributed among members. They shall be transferred to one or more organisations with broadly compatible aims involving recovery, lived experience leadership, community wellbeing, social inclusion or community development.

4._: 12. Adoption and Review — how the Constitution takes effect, and how it is reviewed.
4.1:
12.1 Adoption
This Constitution takes effect when approved by the required vote of Community Recovery members at a properly convened General Meeting.
4.2:
12.2 Review
The Leadership Group should review how the Constitution is working at least annually during the development phase, with particular attention to member participation, volunteer pathways, safeguarding, lived experience leadership and the transition to elections. Changes to the wording must follow Section 10.
